questions.question: What middleware does grid computing typically rely on to coordinate resource sharing across administrative domains?
questions.source_passage: Grid computing is a distributed computing paradigm that pools together the processing, storage, and network resources of geographically distributed, often heterogeneous and independently administered computers... and typically relies on middleware (e.g., Globus Toolkit) to coordinate resource sharing across administrative domains.

questions.question: From a business perspective, how does cloud computing transform IT spending on physical hardware into ongoing operational costs?
questions.source_passage: Converts capital expenditure (CapEx) on hardware/infrastructure into operational expenditure (OpEx) — pay-as-you-go pricing. Faster time-to-market — new applications and services can be launched quickly without procurement/installation delays.

questions.question: What deployment model combines two or more distinct cloud infrastructures to enable data portability and cloud bursting for load balancing?
questions.source_passage: | Hybrid Cloud | A composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private, community, or public) bound together by standardized technology enabling data/application portability (e.g., cloud bursting for load balancing). |

questions.question: What role do Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) play in Amazon EC2 virtual server deployment?
questions.source_passage: Amazon EC2 is an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) offering from Amazon Web Services (AWS) that provides resizable virtual server instances ('instances') in the cloud... Key features include Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) as instance templates, elastic scaling via Auto Scaling groups, multiple instance types optimized for compute/memory/storage-intensive workloads

questions.question: How does Google App Engine (GAE) handle application scaling and infrastructure management for developers?
questions.source_passage: Google App Engine (GAE) is a fully managed Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offering that lets developers build and deploy applications on Google's infrastructure without managing the underlying servers. Developers write code in supported languages (Python, Java, Go, Node.js, etc.), and GAE automatically handles provisioning, scaling (including scaling to zero), load balancing, and patching.

questions.question: In the Platform as a Service (PaaS) model, what layers of the computing stack remain under the customer's direct management?
questions.source_passage: | PaaS (Platform as a Service) | A managed platform (runtime, OS, middleware) for developing/deploying applications | Application code and data only | Google App Engine, Azure App Service, Heroku |

questions.question: How does Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) support composability and reuse when building complex cloud applications?
questions.source_passage: Reusability — common services (e.g., a payment-processing service) can be reused across multiple applications, reducing development effort. Interoperability — standard protocols (REST, SOAP, HTTP/JSON) allow heterogeneous cloud services and legacy systems to interoperate. Composability — complex cloud applications are composed ('orchestrated') from simpler, independently scalable services — closely related to today's microservices architecture.

questions.question: What is Information Life Cycle Management (ILM) in cloud computing, and how does it align storage policies with data value over time?
questions.source_passage: Information Life Cycle Management is a strategy for managing data throughout its useful life — from creation to eventual deletion — by aligning the storage, protection, and access policies applied to data with its changing business value and access frequency over time.

questions.question: How does Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) deliver user desktops from central datacenter servers to client endpoints?
questions.source_passage: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure is a technology that hosts desktop operating systems and applications as virtual machines on centralized servers (in a datacenter or cloud), streaming the desktop's display to end-user devices (thin clients, laptops, tablets) over the network, rather than running the OS locally.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between object storage and block storage in terms of data organization and access methods?
questions.source_passage: Object storage — stores data as discrete objects with metadata, accessed via APIs (e.g., Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage); ideal for unstructured data like images, videos, and backups, offering very high scalability and durability. Block storage — presents raw storage volumes (like a virtual hard disk) attached to virtual machines (e.g., Amazon EBS, Azure Managed Disks); used for databases and applications needing low-latency, high-performance storage.

questions.question: Why is fault tolerance critical in cloud environments running on commodity hardware components?
questions.source_passage: Fault tolerance in cloud computing is the ability of a cloud-based system to continue operating correctly, without interruption or with only minimal degradation, even when one or more of its components (servers, storage devices, network links, or even entire datacenters) fail. It is essential because cloud environments run on large numbers of commodity hardware components, where individual failures are common and expected rather than exceptional.

questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between a Host-based VMM (Type 2 hypervisor) and a Native VMM (Bare-Metal Type 1 hypervisor)?
questions.source_passage:
| Host-based VMM (Hosted Hypervisor) | Native VMM (Bare-Metal Hypervisor) |
| A hypervisor (Type 2) that runs as an application on top of a conventional host operating system | A hypervisor (Type 1) that runs directly on the physical hardware, without a host OS underneath |
